facts.text: Aerospace practice accepts simulation and prior evidence under strict similarity rules: the FAA allows validated models and service history to support similar designs or systems, DO-178C and DO-330 govern airborne software and evidence-producing tools, and MIL-STD-3022 provides a US defense template for documenting model verification, validation and accreditation.
facts.quote: Aviation accepts simulation and prior evidence under strict rules:

facts.text: FAA Advisory Circular 20-146A, dated June 2018, concerns certifying aircraft seats by analysis and is the booklet's clearest example of simulation as compliance evidence.
facts.quote: The FAA's clearest example of simulation as compliance evidence is Advisory Circular 20-146A (June 2018) on certifying aircraft seats by analysis.

facts.text: Under FAA Advisory Circular 20-146A, a baseline aircraft seat must pass physical dynamic tests, and its model must be validated against those tests using criteria agreed in advance.
facts.quote: A baseline seat must pass physical dynamic tests; the model is validated against them with criteria agreed in advance;

facts.text: FAA Advisory Circular 20-146A permits eligible modifications within the same aircraft-seat family to be substantiated by simulation after baseline physical testing and model validation.
facts.quote: eligible modifications within the same family may then be substantiated by simulation;

facts.text: Under FAA Advisory Circular 20-146A, aircraft-seat changes that alter load paths, failure mechanisms, materials or interfaces require new tests.
facts.quote: changes that alter load paths, failure mechanisms, materials or interfaces require new tests;

facts.text: FAA Advisory Circular 20-146A limits model extrapolation to conditions similar to those used for validation.
facts.quote: extrapolation is limited to conditions similar to the validation.

facts.text: FAA AC 25.1309-1B and AC 00-72 accept satisfactory service history as evidence for systems sufficiently similar to a fielded system, provided the differences are identified and justified.
facts.quote: AC 25.1309-1B and AC 00-72 accept satisfactory service history as evidence for systems sufficiently similar to a fielded one, provided the differences are identified and justified

facts.text: DO-178C is the standard for software in airborne systems.
facts.quote: DO-178C is the standard for software in airborne systems;

facts.text: DO-330 is the DO-178C supplement on tool qualification and qualifies tools whose output is relied on without further checking.
facts.quote: DO-330 is its supplement on tool qualification, which qualifies tools whose output is relied on without further checking

facts.text: The booklet notes that DO-330 does not address whether a physics model is valid.
facts.quote: the booklet notes, does not address whether a physics model is valid.

facts.text: MIL-STD-3022 is the US Department of Defense standard for documenting verification, validation and accreditation (VV&A) of models and simulations.
facts.quote: MIL-STD-3022 is the US Department of Defense standard for documenting the verification, validation and accreditation (VV&A) of models and simulations.

facts.text: The booklet names DO-178C, DO-330 and MIL-STD-3022 but did not verify these three standards.
facts.quote: The booklet names all three but did not verify them [Chapter 10].

facts.text: FAA aircraft-seat guidance is the booklet's clearest precedent for using a physical anchor plus virtual variants.
facts.quote: The FAA seat guidance is the booklet's clearest "physical anchor plus virtual variants" precedent

facts.text: The booklet derives a rule for the collision-mitigation validation program from FAA seat guidance: calibration is not validation.
facts.quote: the source of two rules for the program: calibration is not validation

facts.text: The booklet derives a rule for the collision-mitigation validation program from FAA seat guidance: agreement with another model does not validate a model.
facts.quote: a model is not validated by agreement with another model.

facts.text: The FAA seat guidance's 10% tolerances apply to seats and must not be copied to braking validation.
facts.quote: Its 10% tolerances belong to seats and must not be copied to braking [Chapter 10].

facts.text: When simulation results become safety evidence, simulator errors can mask defects.
facts.quote: If simulation results become safety evidence, the simulator is a tool whose errors can mask defects

facts.text: When simulation results become safety evidence, tool qualification must be budgeted as work in the collision-mitigation validation program.
